title: Coral Castle
summary: The mysterious stone sculpture garden built single-handedly by a 100-pound Latvian immigrant who claimed to know the secrets of the Egyptian pyramids - including a 9-ton revolving gate that swings open with the push of a finger.

content.intro: In Homestead, Florida, a diminutive Latvian immigrant spent 28 years carving 1,100 tons of coral rock into a sculpture garden that defies explanation. Edward Leedskalnin stood five feet tall, weighed 100 pounds, and worked only at night, alone. He quarried, moved, and carved massive stone blocks using methods no one witnessed. When asked how he did it, he claimed to understand the secrets used to build the Egyptian pyramids. The centerpiece is a nine-ton gate that once swung open with the push of a finger - so perfectly balanced that children could move it. Leedskalnin said he built it all for Agnes Scuffs, the 16-year-old Latvian girl who called off their wedding the night before the ceremony. She never came to see it. Coral Castle is a monument to obsessive love, unexplained engineering, and the determination of a man who refused to explain himself. Ed died in 1951, his secrets intact.

sections.title: The Builder
sections.body: Edward Leedskalnin was born in Riga, Latvia, in 1887. When he was 26, his fiancée, Agnes Scuffs - ten years his junior - cancelled their wedding the night before the ceremony. Ed never recovered. He emigrated to America, wandered through Canada and Texas, and eventually settled in Florida, where he began quarrying coral limestone and building a monument to his 'Sweet Sixteen.' He worked alone, always at night, using tools he made himself. When visitors came, he stopped working. When asked how he moved the massive stones, he gave cryptic answers about leverage, magnetism, and understanding weight. He charged 10 cents admission and sold pamphlets about his theories on electricity and cosmic forces.

sections.title: The Castle
sections.body: Coral Castle isn't actually coral - it's oolitic limestone, the bedrock underlying much of South Florida. The stones weigh up to 30 tons each. Leedskalnin carved them into furniture, walls, towers, and sculptures: a throne room, a sun dial, a telescope aimed at Polaris, a table shaped like Florida, a bathtub, a barbecue. Everything is precisely fitted without mortar. The walls stand eight feet high, topped with stones shaped like the crenellations of a medieval castle. The 9-ton revolving gate, perfectly balanced on a metal shaft running through its center, operated flawlessly for decades until it broke in 1986 and required a six-man crew with modern equipment to repair.

sections.title: The Mystery
sections.body: How did a 100-pound man move 30-ton blocks alone? Leedskalnin left no clear answer. His workshop contains tripods, chains, pulleys, and hand tools - equipment that could theoretically move heavy stones with enough time and patience. But neighbors who watched from a distance reported seeing stones 'float' into place. When Leedskalnin moved the entire castle from Florida City to Homestead in 1936 - after zoning changes threatened his privacy - he hired a truck but loaded and unloaded the stones himself while the driver looked away. The most likely explanation is extraordinary patience and clever use of basic mechanics. The more exciting explanation involves antigravity and lost ancient knowledge. Leedskalnin preferred the exciting version.

sections.title: The Legacy
sections.body: Leedskalnin died in 1951, leaving Coral Castle to a nephew who sold it. The property has operated as a tourist attraction ever since, drawing visitors who want to see impossible engineering and hear theories about magnetic currents and reverse polarity. Scientists have studied the site; none have found anything supernatural. The stones are heavy but not unmovable by one determined man with time and leverage. The revolving gate was clever engineering, not magic. But the mystery persists because Leedskalnin wanted it to - he spent 28 years building a monument to lost love and refused to explain how, leaving visitors to wonder forever.

sections.title: Visiting Coral Castle
sections.body: Coral Castle is located at 28655 South Dixie Highway in Homestead, Florida, about 30 miles south of Miami. The site is open daily; admission is charged. Guided tours explain the history and demonstrate the features - what remains of the revolving gate's balance, the precision of the sun dial, the acoustic properties of the throne room. The gift shop sells Leedskalnin's pamphlets, reprinted. Homestead is accessible via US-1 from Miami. Miami International Airport is 35 miles north. The Everglades are to the west; the Florida Keys begin 25 miles south. The castle is smaller than photographs suggest but no less impressive for its scale.

content.flightContext: Located at 25.50°N, 80.44°W in Homestead, Florida, between Miami and the Florida Keys. From altitude, Coral Castle is not visible - a small compound in the suburban sprawl of southern Miami-Dade County. Homestead Air Reserve Base is 5 miles east. The Everglades spread west. Biscayne Bay is visible to the east, the Keys stretching south. Miami International Airport is 35 miles north. The terrain is flat limestone barely above sea level, typical of South Florida. The Florida Turnpike and US-1 provide ground access from Miami.
